questions.question: In September 2025, what principle did the Supreme Court affirm in Competition Commission of India v. Kerala Film Exhibitors Federation?

options.text: CCI may impose only monetary fines on enterprises
CCI may impose remedies and fix liability on office-bearers
CCI orders need prior clearance from the Union Cabinet
CCI may drop cases against trade bodies at its discretion

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**CCI may impose remedies and fix liability on office-bearers**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• In the landmark litigation involving the **Competition Commission of India (CCI)** and the **Kerala Film Exhibitors Federation**, the **Supreme Court** affirmed the regulatory power to hold individual leaders of trade bodies accountable for **anti-competitive** conduct.
 
• The core of this principle lies in **Section 48** of the **Competition Act, 2002**, which deals with the **liability of persons in charge** of companies or associations found in contravention of the law.
 
• The Court clarified that an **association of persons** or a **trade federation** falls under the definition of a **'company'** for the purposes of **Section 48**, allowing the **CCI** to look behind the corporate veil.
 
• This ensures that **office-bearers**, including **Presidents**, **Secretaries**, and **Directors**, cannot evade responsibility if they were responsible for the conduct of the association's business at the time of the violation.
 
• The affirmation allows the **CCI** to impose **personal penalties** (usually a percentage of their income) and **behavioral remedies** on these individuals to deter the practice of using federations to orchestrate **boycotts** or **restrictive trade practices**.
 
• By fixing **individual liability**, the ruling prevents trade associations from acting as a front for **cartelization** or **market distortion**, ensuring effective enforcement of **competition law** in fragmented industries like the film exhibition sector.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Competition Act, 2002**:

 
 
• Established the **CCI** to prevent practices having an **adverse effect on competition** (AAEC).
 
• **Section 3**: Prohibits **anti-competitive agreements**, including **horizontal agreements** like cartels.
 
• **Section 4**: Prohibits the **abuse of dominant position** by an enterprise or group.
 
• **Section 27**: Empowers the **CCI** to issue **cease and desist** orders and impose significant **monetary penalties** on both enterprises and individuals.
 
• The Act was amended via the **Competition (Amendment) Act, 2023**, which further expanded the scope of penalties to include **global turnover** for certain violations.
 
 
 
• **Vicarious Liability**:
 
 
• Under **Section 48(2)**, if it is proved that the contravention took place with the **consent**, **connivance**, or **neglect** of any officer, such officer is deemed guilty.
 
• This legal mechanism is vital for maintaining **market integrity** by targeting the **decision-makers** within **non-profit** or **trade-related** organizations.

questions.question: Which article of the Indian Constitution contains the provision for the Council of Ministers to aid and advise the President in the exercise of his powers?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 74**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Article 74(1)** of the **Indian Constitution** explicitly states that there shall be a **Council of Ministers** with the **Prime Minister** at the head to aid and advise the **President**.
 
• The **President** is constitutionally mandated to exercise his functions in accordance with the advice tendered by the Council, highlighting the **Parliamentary form of government** where the President is the **titular head** (De Jure) and the Council is the **real executive** (De Facto).
 
• The **42nd Amendment Act, 1976**, made the advice of the Council of Ministers **binding** on the President.
 
• The **44th Amendment Act, 1978**, introduced a proviso allowing the President to return the advice for **reconsideration** once; however, the President must act according to the advice tendered after such reconsideration.
 
• **Article 74(2)** provides a constitutional shield by stating that the question of whether any, and if so what, advice was tendered by Ministers to the President shall not be inquired into in any **court of law**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Article 64**:

 
 
• Specifies that the **Vice-President** of India shall be the **ex-officio Chairman** of the **Council of States** (Rajya Sabha).
 
• It also mandates that the Vice-President shall not hold any other **office of profit**.
 
 
 
• **Article 84**:
 
 
• Outlines the **qualifications** for becoming a member of **Parliament**.
 
• Key requirements include being a **citizen of India** and meeting age criteria: **25 years** for the **Lok Sabha** and **30 years** for the **Rajya Sabha**.
 
 
 
• **Article 94**:
 
 
• Deals with the **vacation, resignation**, and **removal** from the offices of the **Speaker** and **Deputy Speaker** of the House of the People.
 
• It mentions that the Speaker may resign by writing to the Deputy Speaker and vice versa.
 
 

Therefore, the provision for the Council of Ministers to aid and advise the President is contained in Article 74, which is **Option 4**

questions.question: In which regions of India has canal irrigation seen the most extensive expansion?

options.text: Areas with heavy rainfall and steep slopes

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Alluvial plains with perennial rivers**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Canal irrigation is most extensively developed in the **Northern Plains** of India, particularly in states like **Uttar Pradesh**, **Punjab**, and **Haryana**.
 
• The **Alluvial Plains** are characterized by deep, soft soil layers deposited by rivers, which make the digging of canals and the construction of **distributaries** physically easier and more cost-effective compared to rocky terrains.
 
• The presence of **Perennial Rivers**, such as the **Ganga**, **Yamuna**, and the tributaries of the **Indus**, provides a guaranteed water supply throughout the year, sustaining agricultural activities across different seasons.
 
• The **flat topography** of these plains allows for the distribution of water over large distances through the force of **gravity**, eliminating the high energy costs associated with lifting water.
 
• These regions have a high **water table** and fertile soil, making the massive capital investment in **large-scale canal networks** economically viable for maximizing food grain production.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Types of Canals**:

 
 
• **Inundation Canals**: These are drawn directly from rivers without the use of any barrage or dam and provide water only when the river is in flood.
 
• **Perennial Canals**: These are fed by **dams** or **barrages** built across perennial rivers to regulate and ensure a steady water flow year-round.
 
 
 
• **Regional Constraints**:
 
 
• In the **Peninsular Plateau**, the presence of hard **crystalline rocks** and an undulating landscape makes canal excavation difficult, leading to the dominance of **Tank Irrigation**.
 
• The **Indira Gandhi Canal** project is a notable exception where water is transported from the **Sutlej River** to the arid regions of **Rajasthan**, significantly altering the local **Thar Desert** ecosystem.
 
• Coastal regions often face issues with **salinity** and sandy soil textures that lead to high water **seepage**, making canal transport less efficient than in clay-rich alluvial zones.

questions.question: At the 57th meeting of the **Monetary Policy Committee (MPC)** of the RBI held from 29 September to 1 October 2025, what decision was taken on the policy repo rate and stance?

options.text: Repo rate hiked to 6.00% with a hawkish monetary policy stance
Repo rate kept at 5.50% with a neutral monetary policy stance
Repo rate kept at 5.00% with a calibrated tightening stance
Repo rate cut to 4.50% with an accommodative stance

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Repo rate kept at 5.50% with a neutral monetary policy stance**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **57th meeting** of the **Monetary Policy Committee (MPC)** was conducted from **September 29 to October 1, 2025**, under the chairmanship of **RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra**.
 
• The committee voted unanimously to maintain the **policy repo rate** under the liquidity adjustment facility (LAF) at **5.50%**.
 
• The **MPC** also decided to retain the **monetary policy stance** as **neutral** to remain flexible while ensuring that **inflation** aligns with the target while supporting **economic growth**.
 
• The **Standing Deposit Facility (SDF)** rate remained unchanged at **5.25%**, while the **Marginal Standing Facility (MSF)** rate and the **Bank Rate** were kept steady at **5.75%**.
 
• The decision to hold rates follows a period of **monetary easing** earlier in **2025**, where the **repo rate** was reduced by 100 basis points from 6.50% to 5.50% across the February, April, and June meetings.
 
• During this meeting, the **RBI** revised the **Real GDP growth** projection for **FY 2025-26** upwards to **6.8%** from the previous estimate of 6.5%, driven by robust **domestic demand** and **government capital expenditure**.
 
• The **Consumer Price Index (CPI)** inflation forecast for **FY 2025-26** was revised downwards to **2.6%** (from 3.1%) due to **softening food prices** and the impact of **GST rate rationalization**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Monetary Policy Stance Definitions:**

 
 
• **Neutral Stance:** Indicates that the central bank is comfortable with current **interest rates** and can move in either direction (hike or cut) based on incoming **economic data** and **global uncertainty**.
 
• **Accommodative Stance:** A posture where the central bank is prepared to **expand the money supply** and **cut rates** to stimulate **economic activity**.
 
• **Hawkish Stance:** A focus on **controlling inflation** as the top priority, often leading to **higher interest rates** to reduce **liquidity**.
 
• **Calibrated Tightening:** A stance indicating that **rate hikes** are on the table, but **rate cuts** are ruled out for the immediate future.
 
 
 
• **MPC Composition:** The **Monetary Policy Committee** consists of six members: three from the **Reserve Bank of India** and three external members appointed by the **Government of India**. Decisions are made by a **majority vote**, with the **Governor** having a casting vote in case of a tie.
 
• **Policy Corridor:** The **SDF** and **MSF** rates represent the floor and ceiling of the **interest rate corridor**, which is positioned 25 basis points below and above the **repo rate**, respectively.

questions.question: On April 9, 2025, the Reserve Bank of India's Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) announced a cut in the repo rate by:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**25 basis points**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• During the **54th meeting** of the **Monetary Policy Committee (MPC)** held from **April 7 to 9, 2025**, the committee unanimously voted to reduce the policy **repo rate** by **25 basis points**.
 
• With this 25 bps cut, the benchmark repo rate was brought down from 6.25% to **6.00%** with immediate effect.
 
• The decision was taken under the chairmanship of the RBI Governor, **Sanjay Malhotra**, marking the first bi-monthly monetary policy statement of the financial year **2025-26**.
 
• Consequently, the **Standing Deposit Facility (SDF)** rate was adjusted to **5.75%**, while the **Marginal Standing Facility (MSF)** rate and the **Bank Rate** were adjusted to **6.25%**.
 
• The MPC also unanimously decided to shift its policy stance to **accommodative** to support domestic economic growth amidst escalating global trade challenges and protectionist tariff regimes.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Repo Rate (Repurchasing Option)**:

 
 
• It is the key policy interest rate at which the **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)** lends short-term money to commercial banks, typically against collateral of government securities.
 
• A lower repo rate makes borrowing cheaper for banks, which in turn leads to lower lending rates (EMIs) for home, auto, and other consumer loans.
 
 
 
• **Monetary Policy Committee (MPC)**:
 
 
• The MPC is a **six-member statutory body** constituted under Section 45ZB of the amended **Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934**.
 
• It is responsible for determining the policy interest rates required to achieve the inflation target of **4%** within a band of plus/minus **2%**.
 
• It consists of three internal members (including the **RBI Governor** as ex-officio Chairperson) and three external members appointed by the **Government of India**.
 
 
 
• **Key Monetary Policy Instruments**:
 
 
• **Standing Deposit Facility (SDF)**: The rate at which the RBI absorbs liquidity from commercial banks without any collateral. It acts as the lower bound of the policy corridor.
 
• **Marginal Standing Facility (MSF)**: A penal rate at which commercial banks can borrow emergency overnight funds from the RBI by dipping into their statutory liquidity ratio (SLR) portfolio.
 
• **Basis Points (bps)**: A financial unit of measure equal to one-hundredth of a percentage point (0.01%). Thus, a 25 basis point change is equal to a 0.25% change.

questions.question: Which case recognised judicial review as part of the basic structure?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Keshavananda Bharati case**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Keshavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)** case is a landmark judgment in Indian constitutional law where a **13-judge bench**, the largest ever constituted, delivered a verdict with a **7:6 majority**.
 
• This case propounded the **Basic Structure Doctrine**, ruling that while **Parliament** has the power to amend the **Constitution** under **Article 368**, it cannot alter its essential features or fundamental framework.
 
• The judgment established that the **Supremacy of the Constitution** and the **Separation of Powers** are core elements; since **Judicial Review** is the mechanism used by the judiciary to interpret these laws, it is inherently part of the **basic structure**.
 
• The court held that the power of **amendment** is not the power to **abrogate** the Constitution, thereby ensuring that the **Judicial Review** power of the **Supreme Court** and **High Courts** remains intact to check legislative overreach.
 
• By limiting the amending power of **Parliament**, the case ensured that the **Judiciary** remains the final arbiter of constitutional validity, effectively recognizing **Judicial Review** as an indestructible pillar of the **Indian Democracy**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Minerva Mills case (1980)**:

 
 
• This case further clarified the **Basic Structure Doctrine** by striking down portions of the **42nd Amendment Act**.
 
• The court explicitly held that **Judicial Review** and a **limited amending power** are fundamental features that cannot be taken away.
 
 
 
• **Menaka Gandhi case (1978)**:
 
 
• Significantly expanded the scope of **Article 21** (Right to Life and Personal Liberty).
 
• Established the principle that any law depriving a person of their liberty must satisfy the triple test of being **prescribed by law**, having a **legitimate aim**, and being **just, fair, and reasonable**.
 
 
 
• **Indra Sawhney case (1992)**:
 
 
• Commonly known as the **Mandal Commission case**, it examined the scope of **Article 16(4)** regarding **reservations**.
 
• The court upheld **27% reservation** for **Other Backward Classes (OBCs)** but introduced the **creamy layer** concept and a **50% ceiling** on total reservations.

questions.question: The Naval Anti-Ship missile *(***NASM‑SR)**, tested in February 2025, has what special feature?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Man-in-loop retargeting via infrared seeker**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Naval Anti-Ship Missile-Short Range (NASM-SR)** is the first indigenous air-launched anti-ship missile system developed by the **Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO)** specifically for the **Indian Navy**.
 
• The missile is equipped with a highly advanced **Imaging Infrared (IIR)** seeker, which enables it to home in on the thermal signature of enemy vessels, providing high-resolution imagery for target discrimination.
 
• The **Man-in-loop (MIL)** feature is a critical technological highlight that provides a real-time data link between the missile and the operator, allowing for **retargeting** or the selection of a specific impact point on the ship after launch.
 
• The flight test conducted in **February 2025** successfully demonstrated the seamless integration of this seeker-link technology, confirming the missile’s high precision and lethality in complex maritime environments.
 
• Designed for launch from maritime helicopters like the **Sikorsky MH-60R** and **Sea King**, the missile effectively bridges the gap in the Navy’s short-range offensive capabilities against corvette-class vessels and patrol boats.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Guidance and Stealth**:

 
 
• Unlike radar-guided missiles, the **IIR seeker** is a **passive guidance** system, meaning it does not emit signals that can be detected by the target ship’s **Electronic Support Measures (ESM)**, making the missile stealthier.
 
• The missile utilizes a combination of **Inertial Navigation System (INS)** and **satellite navigation (GPS/NavIC)** for mid-course guidance before the seeker takes over for the terminal phase.
 
 
 
• **Operational Performance**:
 
 
• The **NASM-SR** has an operational range of approximately **55 kilometers** and travels at **subsonic speeds**, optimized for sea-skimming flight to evade enemy defenses.
 
• It is powered by a **solid-propellant rocket motor** and carries a specialized **semi-armor-piercing warhead** designed to penetrate the thick hulls of naval targets.

questions.question: According to the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA) RE Statistics 2025, India holds the 3rd global rank in the** installed capacity **of which renewable energy category?

• **Global Integration**: The **1991 Economic Reforms** aimed to integrate the Indian economy with the global market. This was achieved by reducing **import duties**, encouraging **Foreign Direct Investment (FDI)**, and aligning domestic policies with **World Trade Organization (WTO)** standards.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

• In India, it was initiated under the **New Economic Policy** of **1991** by the government of **P.V. Narasimha Rao** and Finance Minister **Dr. Manmohan Singh**.
 
• The core pillars were **Liberalization**, **Privatization**, and **Globalization** (LPG).
 
 
 
• **Impact on the Indian Economy**:
 
 
• Significant increase in the **Gross Domestic Product (GDP)** growth rate.
 
• Growth of the **Service Sector**, contributing to over 50% of India's GDP.
 
• Expansion of **Foreign Exchange Reserves** and better access to international capital markets.

questions.question: Which computing pioneer is credited with the concept of the "stored program architecture" (where both program instructions and data are held in the same memory), a design that forms the basis of nearly all modern computers?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**John von Neumann**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **John von Neumann** was a Hungarian-American mathematician who formalized the concept of the **stored-program computer** in his influential **1945** document, **First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC**.
 
• The **von Neumann architecture**, also known as the **Princeton architecture**, is based on the principle that **program instructions** and **data** are stored in the same **read-write, random-access memory (RAM)**.
 
• This design allows the **Central Processing Unit (CPU)** to fetch instructions and data using the same **bus** system, fundamentally simplifying the hardware required to switch between different computational tasks.
 
• Before this innovation, machines like the **ENIAC** had to be manually **re-plugged** and **rewired** to execute different programs, making them **fixed-program** computers rather than general-purpose machines.
 
• The architecture consists of four main sub-systems: the **Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU)**, the **Control Unit**, the **Memory**, and **Input/Output (I/O)** devices.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Alan Turing**:

 
 
• Commonly recognized as the **Father of Modern Computer Science**, he developed the theoretical model of the **Turing Machine** and the **Universal Turing Machine**.
 
• While he worked on early stored-program designs like the **Automatic Computing Engine (ACE)**, the specific architecture defining modern hardware is traditionally attributed to von Neumann.

questions.question: Which of the following is the correct full form of CD?

__
 
• The acronym **CD** stands for **Compact Disk** (alternatively spelled as **Compact Disc**), which is a digital **optical disc** data storage format.
 
• It was co-developed by **Philips** and **Sony** and was first commercially released in **1982**, primarily intended for digital audio recordings.
 
• The technology utilizes a **polycarbonate** plastic substrate coated with a thin layer of **aluminum** to reflect laser light; data is stored as a series of microscopic indentations known as **pits** and flat areas called **lands**.
 
• A standard **Compact Disk** has a diameter of **120 millimeters** and can store up to **700 MB** of data or approximately **80 minutes** of uncompressed high-fidelity audio.
 
• The reading process involves a **semiconductor laser** with a wavelength of **780 nm** that detects the changes in reflectivity between pits and lands as the disc spins.
 
• Therefore, **Option (4)** is the correct answer as it accurately represents the technical name for this storage medium.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Computer Drive**: While a **CD drive** is a type of computer drive, the acronym CD itself specifically refers to the storage medium (the disk) rather than the mechanical drive assembly.
 
• **Variations of Compact Disks**:
 
 
• **CD-ROM**: Standing for **Read-Only Memory**, these are pre-pressed discs used for distributing software and games.
 
• **CD-R**: A **Recordable** format that allows a user to write data once using a laser to burn a dye layer, after which the data cannot be erased.
 
• **CD-RW**: A **Re-Writable** format that uses a **phase-change** metallic alloy, allowing the data to be erased and rewritten approximately 1,000 times.
 
 
 
• **Technological Succession**: The **Compact Disk** laid the foundation for subsequent optical formats like the **DVD** (Digital Versatile Disc) and **Blu-ray Disc**, which use shorter wavelength lasers to achieve much higher storage densities.

__
 
• **RFID (Radio Frequency Identification)** is a computer-driven technology that uses electromagnetic fields to automatically identify and track tags attached to objects, making it the primary tool for **real-time inventory tracking**.
 
• Unlike traditional barcoding, **RFID** does not require a direct **line-of-sight** to read information, allowing for the simultaneous scanning of hundreds of items as they move through a **warehouse** or distribution center.
 
• This application falls under the category of **AIDC (Automatic Identification and Data Capture)**, which minimizes human intervention and significantly reduces errors in **supply chain management** and logistics.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **System Components**:

questions.question: Modern telecommunication systems use optical fibres to transmit data efficiently. Which optical phenomenon enables this high-speed data transmission?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Total Internal Reflection**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Total Internal Reflection (TIR)** is the fundamental principle that allows **optical fibres** to guide light over long distances with minimal signal loss.
 
• An optical fibre consists of a central **Core** surrounded by a layer called **Cladding**. For TIR to occur, the **refractive index** of the core (n₁) must be higher than the refractive index of the cladding (n₂).
 
• When a light signal (representing data) is launched into the fibre, it strikes the interface between the core and the cladding at an **angle of incidence** that is greater than the **critical angle**.
 
• Because the angle exceeds the critical threshold, the light does not exit the core through **refraction** but is entirely reflected back into the denser medium of the core.
 
• This process repeats thousands of times per meter, effectively trapping the light pulse inside the fibre and allowing it to travel at **high speeds** through curved or straight paths.
 
• The efficiency of **Total Internal Reflection** ensures that nearly 100 percent of the light energy remains confined, which is crucial for maintaining **signal integrity** in modern **telecommunication systems**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Dispersion of light**

 
 
• This refers to the splitting of light into its constituent spectral colors.
 
• In fibre optics, **chromatic dispersion** can lead to pulse broadening, which actually acts as a limitation to **bandwidth** rather than a means of transmission.
 
 
 
• **Refraction of light**
 
 
• Refraction involves the bending of light as it passes from one medium to another.
 
• While refraction is used to initially couple light into the fibre, the goal of the fibre design is to avoid refraction at the **core-cladding boundary** to prevent light leakage.
 
 
 
• **Interference of light**
 
 
• Interference is the phenomenon where two waves superpose to form a resultant wave of greater, lower, or the same amplitude.
 
• It is utilized in **interferometers** and specific sensors but is not the primary mechanism for guiding light through a standard **telecommunication fibre**.

questions.question: A student mixes aqueous solutions of barium chloride and sodium sulphate. A white curd-like substance forms instantly. What type of chemical reaction is primarily responsible for this observation?

options.text: Precipitation reaction forming insoluble barium sulphate
Redox reaction resulting in electron transfer
Decomposition of sodium sulphate by barium chloride catalyst
Evolution of SO₂ gas during a displacement reaction

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Precipitation reaction forming insoluble barium sulphate**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• When aqueous solutions of **Barium chloride** and **Sodium sulphate** are mixed, a chemical reaction occurs where the **Barium ions** ( Ba²⁺ ) from the barium chloride react with the **Sulphate ions** ( SO₄²− ) from the sodium sulphate.
 
• The balanced chemical equation for this process is: BaCl₂(aq) + Na₂SO₄(aq) rightarrow BaSO₄(s) + 2NaCl(aq) .
 
• This reaction is specifically classified as a **double displacement reaction** because the positive and negative ions of the two ionic compounds exchange partners to form two new compounds.
 
• The **Barium sulphate** ( BaSO₄ ) produced is an **insoluble salt** that does not dissolve in water and settles out of the solution as a white, curd-like solid.
 
• In chemistry, any reaction that produces an **insoluble solid** (precipitate) upon mixing two aqueous solutions is defined as a **precipitation reaction**.
 
• The other product, **Sodium chloride** ( NaCl ), remains dissolved in the aqueous solution as it is highly soluble.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Redox Reaction**

 
 
• Involves a change in **oxidation states** of atoms through the **transfer of electrons**.
 
• In the reaction between barium chloride and sodium sulphate, the oxidation states of all elements remain constant; therefore, it is not a **redox process**.
 
 
 
• **Decomposition Reaction**
 
 
• A process where a single reactant breaks down into two or more simpler products, often requiring **thermal energy**, **light**, or **electricity**.
 
• This scenario involves two distinct reactants forming two new products, which contradicts the definition of **decomposition**.
 
 
 
• **Evolution of Gas**
 
 
• Certain reactions result in the release of gaseous products like SO₂ or CO₂ .
 
• The mixing of these specific salt solutions does not involve any **effervescence** or the formation of **Sulphur dioxide** gas; the only visible change is the formation of a **solid precipitate**.

questions.question: What type of joint allows the widest range of movement, including medial and lateral rotation, as in the shoulder and hip?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Ball and Socket Joint**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• A **Ball and Socket Joint** is a specialized type of **synovial joint** where the rounded, ball-like surface of one bone fits into the cup-like depression (socket) of another bone.
 
• It is classified as a **multiaxial joint** (or triaxial), which means it allows movement in three primary planes: **anterior-posterior**, **medial-lateral**, and **rotational**.
 
• This joint structure provides the **widest range of movement** of all joint types in the human body, facilitating **flexion**, **extension**, **abduction**, **adduction**, and **circumduction**.
 
• Specifically, it enables both **medial rotation** (inward) and **lateral rotation** (outward), which are critical for the functionality of the limbs.
 
• The most prominent examples are the **Shoulder Joint** (glenohumeral joint), where the head of the humerus meets the glenoid cavity, and the **Hip Joint** (acetabulofemoral joint), where the femur head meets the acetabulum.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Hinge Joint**:

 
 
• Characterized as a **uniaxial joint** that functions like a door hinge, allowing movement in only one plane.
 
• Primary actions are **flexion** and **extension**; found in the **Elbow**, **Knee**, and **Interphalangeal joints** of the fingers.
 
 
 
• **Pivot Joint**:
 
 
• A **uniaxial joint** that allows only **rotation** around a single longitudinal axis.
 
• Examples include the **Atlanto-axial joint** (between the first two vertebrae) and the **Proximal radioulnar joint**.
 
 
 
• **Gliding Joint**:
 
 
• Also known as a **Plane Joint**, where the articulating surfaces are flat or slightly curved.
 
• Allows bones to slide over each other with minimal rotation; found between the **Carpal bones** of the wrist and **Tarsal bones** of the foot.

questions.question: What modification was made to Article 171(1) of the Indian Constitution by the seventh amendment?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Term 'one-fourth' was replaced with 'one-third'**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Article 171** of the **Constitution of India** deals with the composition of the **Legislative Councils** (Vidhan Parishad) in the states.
 
• Prior to the 1956 amendment, **Article 171(1)** stipulated that the total number of members in the **Legislative Council** of a State should not exceed **one-fourth** of the total number of members in the **Legislative Assembly** of that State.
 
• The **Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, 1956**, was enacted primarily to implement the **States Reorganisation Act**, which restructured state boundaries on a linguistic basis.
 
• Section 10 of this amendment specifically modified **Article 171(1)** by substituting the word **one-fourth** with **one-third**.
 
• This change allowed for a larger **Legislative Council** in proportion to the **Legislative Assembly**, providing broader representation while ensuring the Council remained the smaller, revisory chamber.
 
• Despite the increase in the maximum limit, the constitutional minimum strength of a **Legislative Council** remained fixed at **40** members.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Composition Details of Legislative Council**:

 
 
• **Elected by Local Bodies**: Approximately **one-third** of the members are elected by members of local authorities like **Municipalities** and **District Boards**.
 
• **Elected by Legislative Assembly**: Another **one-third** are elected by the members of the **Legislative Assembly** from among persons who are not members of the Assembly.
 
• **Elected by Graduates**: About **one-twelfth** are elected by persons residing in the state who have been **graduates** for at least three years.
 
• **Elected by Teachers**: About **one-twelfth** are elected by persons engaged in teaching in **educational institutions** (not lower than secondary schools) for at least three years.
 
• **Nominated by Governor**: The remainder (about **one-sixth**) are nominated by the **Governor** from individuals with special knowledge in **Literature**, **Science**, **Art**, **Co-operative Movement**, and **Social Service**.
 
 
 
• **Legislative Status**:
 
 
• Unlike the **Legislative Assembly**, the **Legislative Council** is a **permanent body** and is not subject to dissolution; however, **one-third** of its members retire every second year.

questions.question: The Eleventh Scheduled of the Constitution places how many functions within the purview of the Panchayati Raj bodies?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**29**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Eleventh Schedule** was added to the **Constitution of India** through the **73rd Constitutional Amendment Act** of **1992**, which provided a formal framework for **Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs)**.
 
• This schedule specifies the powers, authority, and responsibilities of **Panchayats** and contains exactly **29 functional items** or subjects over which these local bodies have jurisdiction.
 
• The inclusion of these 29 functions is mandated under **Article 243G**, which empowers the **State Legislatures** to devolve necessary powers to the **Panchayats** to enable them to function as institutions of self-government.
 
• These functions are intended to ensure **economic development** and **social justice** at the grassroots level by allowing local representatives to manage essential community services and resources.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Core Subjects of the Eleventh Schedule:**

 
 
• **Agriculture and Land:** Includes **agricultural extension**, **land improvement**, implementation of land reforms, and **soil conservation**.
 
• **Water and Resources:** Covers **minor irrigation**, water management, **watershed development**, and providing safe **drinking water**.
 
• **Social Infrastructure:** Encompasses **rural housing**, **roads**, culverts, bridges, and **rural electrification** including distribution of electricity.
 
• **Social Welfare:** Includes **poverty alleviation programs**, **education** (primary and secondary), **adult and non-formal education**, and **libraries**.
 
• **Health and Community:** Manages **health and sanitation** (including hospitals and PHCs), **family welfare**, **women and child development**, and the **Public Distribution System (PDS)**.
 
• **Economic Activities:** Focuses on **fisheries**, **animal husbandry**, **social forestry**, and **small-scale industries** like **Khadi and village industries**.
 
 
 
• **Constitutional Framework:**
 
 
• The **73rd Amendment Act** introduced **Part IX** to the Constitution, titled **The Panchayats**, spanning from **Article 243** to **Article 243O**.
 
• In contrast, the **Twelfth Schedule**, introduced by the **74th Constitutional Amendment Act**, lists **18 functional items** specifically for **Municipalities** in urban areas.

questions.question: Which branch of the monsoon brings rainfall to India’s Western Coast?

options.text: South-West Monsoon Bay of Bengal branch

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**South-West Monsoon Arabian Sea branch**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **South-West Monsoon** is the primary rainy season in India, typically active from **June to September**. It originates due to the intense low-pressure system over the **Thar Desert** and the **Tibetan Plateau**, which draws moisture-laden winds from the high-pressure area over the **Indian Ocean**.
 
• As the monsoon winds approach the **Indian Peninsula**, they are divided into two main branches: the **Arabian Sea branch** and the **Bay of Bengal branch**.
 
• The **Arabian Sea branch** strikes the **Western Coast** of India first, typically hitting the coast of **Kerala** around **June 1st**. This branch is significantly more powerful than the Bay of Bengal branch, carrying approximately **three times** more moisture.
 
• Rainfall on the Western Coast is primarily **orographic** in nature. When the moisture-laden winds encounter the **Western Ghats** (Sahyadri), they are forced to rise. As the air rises, it cools adiabatically, leading to heavy precipitation on the **windward side** (the coastal plains).
 
• Regions such as the **Konkan Coast**, **Malabar Coast**, and the states of **Maharashtra**, **Goa**, **Karnataka**, and **Kerala** receive torrential rainfall, often exceeding **250 cm** annually, due to this specific branch.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **South-West Monsoon Bay of Bengal branch**:

 
 
• This branch moves towards **Northeast India** and the **Ganges Valley**.
 
• It is responsible for the highest rainfall in the world at **Mawsynram** and **Cherrapunji** on the **Khasi Hills**.
 
 
 
• **North-East Monsoon**:
 
 
• Also known as the **Retreating Monsoon**, it occurs during **October and November**.
 
• The winds blow from the land to the sea, picking up moisture from the **Bay of Bengal** and providing crucial rainfall to the **Coromandel Coast** (Tamil Nadu).
 
 
 
• **Western Disturbances**:
 
 
• These are **extra-tropical cyclones** originating in the **Mediterranean Sea**.
 
• They bring winter rainfall to **Northwest India** (Punjab, Haryana), which is vital for the **Rabi crops**, specifically **wheat**.

questions.question: Which process mainly helps in the formation of V-shaped valleys in mountainous regions?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**River erosion**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• A **V-shaped valley** is a narrow valley with a cross-section resembling the letter 'V', formed primarily through the action of **River erosion** in high-altitude **mountainous regions**.
 
• In the **youthful stage** of a river, the flow is extremely rapid due to a steep **topographic gradient**, leading to a process known as **vertical erosion** or **downcutting**.
 
• The **river bed** is eroded downward much faster than the valley walls can be eroded laterally, which creates a deep, narrow channel.
 
• As the river deepens, the exposed valley sides are subjected to **mechanical weathering** and **mass wasting** (such as soil creep and landslides), which gradually widen the top of the valley while the base remains narrow.
 
• The combination of constant **downward incision** by the water and the outward collapse of the slopes results in the characteristic **V-shaped profile**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Wind erosion**:

 
 
• Primarily occurs in **arid and semi-arid** environments where vegetation is sparse.
 
• It creates landforms such as **Mushroom rocks**, **Inselbergs**, and **Yardangs** through processes like **abrasion** and **deflation**.
 
 
 
• **Wave action**:
 
 
• Focuses on **coastal geomorphology** where the energy of the ocean waves erodes shorelines.
 
• Key landforms include **Sea cliffs**, **Stacks**, **Sea caves**, and **Natural arches**.
 
 
 
• **Glacier movement**:
 
 
• Responsible for the formation of **U-shaped valleys** or **glacial troughs**.
 
• Unlike rivers, glaciers are massive ice bodies that erode both the **valley floor** and the **valley walls** simultaneously through **plucking** and **abrasion**, resulting in a wide, flat bottom and steep, straight sides.

• The genre was established in the 13th century by the legendary poet and musician **Amir Khusrau**, who is often referred to as the **Father of Qawwali**.
 
• The primary goal of **Qawwali** is to lead both the performers and the listeners to a state of spiritual ecstasy known as **Wajad** or **Hal**.
 
• A typical performance starts with the **Hamd** (praise of Allah), followed by the **Naat** (praise of Prophet Muhammad), and **Manqabat** (praise of Ali or Sufi saints).
 
• Musically, it involves a lead singer supported by a chorus, rhythmic **hand clapping**, and instruments like the **Harmonium** and **Tabla** or **Dholak** to create a powerful, repetitive rhythmic cycle.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Tarana**:

 
 
• A fast-paced vocal composition in **Hindustani classical music** that uses rhythmic syllables like **odani**, **tanedere**, and **yalali**.
 
• While invented by **Amir Khusrau** with Persian influences, it is now primarily a secular concert piece focused on **Layakari** (rhythmic play).
 
 
 
• **Dhrupad**:
 
 
• The oldest surviving genre of **Hindustani music**, known for its meditative and austere nature, originally performed in **Hindu temples** and later the **Mughal court**.
 
• It features a four-part structure: **Sthayi**, **Antara**, **Sanchari**, and **Abhog**, typically accompanied by the **Pakhawaj**.
 
 
 
• **Tappa**:
 
 
• Developed from the folk songs of **Punjabi camel riders**, it was refined into a classical style by **Shory Mian**.
 
• It is characterized by extremely rapid, complex, and **ornamental melodic phrases** or **taans**.

__
 
• The **Ambubachi Mela** is a prominent Hindu festival held annually at the **Kamakhya Temple** in **Guwahati**, **Assam**, and is considered the most important event of the temple's calendar.
 
• This festival is celebrated during the **monsoon season**, specifically in the middle of **June**, coinciding with the Assamese month of **Ahaar**.
 
• It celebrates the annual **menstrual cycle** of the goddess **Kamakhya**; during this three-day period, the temple remains closed to the public as it is believed the **Mother Earth** is undergoing menstruation.
 
• On the **fourth day**, the temple doors are opened with great fanfare, and devotees are allowed to enter to receive **Prasad** and seek blessings from the goddess.
 
• The festival is popularly known as the **Mahakumbh of the East** because it attracts millions of pilgrims, **Sadhus**, **Tantriks**, and **Bauls** from across India and neighboring countries.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Kamakhya Temple**:

 
 
• Situated atop the **Nilachal Hills**, this temple is one of the **51 Shakti Peethas** and represents the **yoni** (genitals) of Goddess **Sati**.
 
• The temple follows the **Nilachal style** of architecture, featuring a unique hemispherical dome resting on a cruciform base.
 
• It is a primary center for **Tantric Shaktism**, where the deity is worshipped in the form of a natural stone fissure kept moist by a natural spring.
 
 
 
• **Cultural Significance**:
 
 
• The **Ambubachi Mela** promotes the idea of **fertility** and challenges social taboos by openly celebrating the biological process of **menstruation**.
 
• The devotees are often given small pieces of red cloth called **Angodak** as **Prasad**, which is highly sought after for its spiritual significance.
 
• While **Bihar**, **Jharkhand**, and **Chhattisgarh** host significant regional festivals like **Chhath Puja**, **Sarhul**, and **Bastar Dussehra** respectively, they do not observe the **Ambubachi Mela**.

__
 
• **Rabi crops** are agricultural crops that are sown during the winter season, typically starting from **October to December**, and are harvested in the spring season between **April and June**.
 
• **Wheat** is the premier rabi crop in India and is extensively grown in the **Northern** and **Northwestern** regions, including states like **Punjab**, **Haryana**, **Himachal Pradesh**, **Jammu and Kashmir**, **Uttarakhand**, and **Uttar Pradesh**.
 
• The growth of **Wheat** is significantly aided by the **Western Temperate Cyclones**, which bring vital precipitation during the winter months, ensuring a healthy yield for the rabi season.
 
• Other prominent examples of rabi crops include **Barley**, **Peas**, **Gram**, and **Mustard**, all of which require a cool growing season followed by bright sunshine during the ripening phase.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Kharif Crops**: These are monsoon-dependent crops sown at the beginning of the rainy season (**June to July**) and harvested in **September to October**.

 
 
• **Rice**: It is a staple kharif crop requiring high temperatures (above **25°C**), high humidity, and heavy annual rainfall exceeding **100 cm**.
 
• **Cotton**: This is a major commercial kharif crop that thrives in **black cotton soil** and requires at least **210 frost-free days** for optimal growth.
 
• **Bajra**: Also known as pearl millet, it is a kharif crop that grows well in dry climates, sandy soils, and shallow black soils, predominantly in states like **Rajasthan**.
 
 
 
• **Zaid Crops**: These are short-duration crops grown during the summer months between the rabi and kharif seasons (**March to June**), such as **Watermelon**, **Muskmelon**, and **Cucumber**.
